paragraphs.text: Once again the spiritual harp of blessed David, struck by the Holy Spirit, has given you its heavenly sounds. They do not charm the ears; they educate souls. For the work of this holy harp is to sanctify souls. Psalmody is for every occasion: a festival for the cheerful and a comfort for the downhearted. It is a kind of holy incantation, not one recited from myths. It lulls the desires to sleep as if they were evil beasts, banishes licentiousness, quenches injustice, kindles righteousness, overturns blasphemous suspicions, does away with shameful thoughts, dictates the divine law, proclaims God, interprets the faith, muzzles heretics and builds up the Church. Many and varied, then, are the things sung on this holy harp. But today blessed David proclaims the kingship of God, saying: "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad." This is what the first psalm made known to us through the teaching that came before. For the divine readings must be regarded as teaching. What comes from us is not teaching but the interpretation of teaching. And to see that psalmody is also teaching, hear the prophet himself saying: "I will teach the lawless your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you." First he is taught, then he teaches. A reservoir cannot send its waters down to a garden bed or a garden unless it receives an abundant stream. In the same way, unless the prophet and the apostle borrow the divine streams from heavenly grace, they can neither have them themselves nor share them with others. And to see that the prophet is taught, hear him take the place of a disciple when he says: "Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths"; and "Blessed are you, O Lord; teach me your statutes." Do you see how he is taught and then teaches? For every God-loving soul that does not have God cannot be entrusted with teaching. Nothing born of human reasoning is secure, but everything proclaimed by divine Scripture is secure and true. Reasoning knows how both to build up and to tear down. Every human argument can meet with either assent or refusal, but the divine voice shows itself more effective than any deed. That is why God speaks and things come together at once, and the word of God is a heavenly nod. It is no wonder if God commands and something happens among the things that exist, since when he speaks, even things that do not exist are brought into existence. Today, then, blessed David teaches and proclaims God's kingship, saying: "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice." But we need to examine the phrase itself. What does "The Lord has become king" mean? Is it not said of someone who has recently taken up the kingship? No one would say of a king who has reigned for a long time, "The king has become king." What someone has held from long ago, we cannot proclaim as a recent acquisition. What, then, does David mean by saying, "The Lord has become king"? If he always reigns, "has become king" is superfluous. It must be, then, that he meant to hymn a kingship and rightly said "The Lord has become king," as of a kingship that had a beginning. But when does God's kingship begin? Recently? Was there ever a time when God existed but was not king? How could that be? Nothing is new with God. He does not acquire authority or put on kingship. He is king from eternity, master from eternity, creator from eternity, as blessed Moses says: "The Lord reigns forever and ever and beyond." Blessed Moses lived many generations before David and proclaimed God's kingship. Why, then, does blessed David proclaim this ancient kingship as something new, saying, "The Lord has become king"? Clearly he is interpreting the Savior's dispensation. For the Savior's kingship is twofold. One kingship is before the ages and has no beginning. The other comes after the ages and takes its beginning from the dispensation. Although he is always king, he also becomes king according to the flesh. He has the one kingship by nature, and he receives the other through his human formation. Our Savior, then, has become king. And David does not say "The Lord has become king" idly. Before Christ's kingship, other powers reigned in the world. Within it there was, as it were, a kingship of tyrants that did not rule by nature but fell upon creation as a violent lawlessness. The demons reigned over the world, not because they possessed a kingship, but because they had disguised tyranny as kingship. So when he says "The Lord has become king," he is announcing the overthrow of the demons' tyranny and the dispensation that shone forth through the Savior's coming. He means that the Lord drove out the kingship of the demons and brought in his own incarnate and divine dispensation. We must show from the Scriptures themselves what reigned before Christ. Hear Paul saying: "Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned." See, the kingship of death reigned. Elsewhere sin reigned, as the same apostle says: "Do not let sin reign in your mortal body." And: "Just as sin reigned through the one, so also grace reigns through the one." He has shown, then, that before Christ both sin and death reigned, and they succeeded one another like harsh kings and tyrants. Sin reigned in the world. Then, when a man had completed his course of life, he was handed over to the kingship of death, and so the kingship of sin passed him on to the kingship of death. The human race was plundered, passed from tyranny to tyranny and from enemy to enemy. Sin reigned; death succeeded sin and reigned (for "the sting of death," it says, "is sin"), and the human race lay under tyranny. So blessed David brings the oppressed the good news that the king is coming. When people held under a tyrant hear that a king is arriving, the news dispels their dejection and grief and plants good hopes in them. In the same way David brings good news to the earth that is in anguish, trampled, tyrannized and held by demons, saying: "The Lord has become king; let the earth rejoice." When did he become king? When did his kingship begin? According to the flesh, he began the kingship given to him as man. But the kingship that is before the ages had no beginning and will have no end. We have discussed this phrase before, but it is necessary to recall it again. A speaker should not consider only whether he has used a saying once. He should ask whether it needs to be brought forward repeatedly to heal the wound of sin, and if so, say it again.

The children of heretics claim that the Savior received from the Father even the kingship he has, and that he has nothing by nature but everything by grace. It is therefore necessary to show which dispensation was given to him by grace through the flesh, and which kingship belonged to him by nature because of his dignity before the ages. The Savior was established as king by the Father, but not as king of heaven and earth, for he did not receive that kingship by appointment. He was appointed king over the people according to the incarnate dispensation. "For I," it says, "have been established as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain." He came to Judea and received the incarnate dispensation. Though he was the eternal God, he was seen on earth and lived among human beings. Then he received a new kingship, the one that came by succession from David. He did not acquire some other kingship for himself; he took up the one that the house of David had lost. That is why the angel Gabriel says to the virgin Mary: "Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus, for he will save his people." Pay close attention. He had not yet preached or taught, and still the angel says "his people." This is so that you may learn that the people did not become his people only after the Passion. He did not inherit a people after the Passion. He had the people even before the Passion, as Master of the people, and by the Passion he won back the universal Church. "For he will save his people from their sins." "And the Lord will give him" — give whom? The one born of you in the incarnate dispensation. "And the Lord God will give him the throne" — what throne? "Of his father David." He does not receive the heavenly kingship, for he already had it. He recovers this kingship, which the demons had snatched from the house of David. "And the Lord will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end." If the kingdom is eternal and has no end, what room is left for the badly interpreted saying, "When he hands over the kingdom to God the Father"? As I said before, Scripture often uses "kingdom" not only for the dignity of those who reign but also for the nations they rule. For how could there be a king if there were no subjects? So it calls the nation, the people, the world under the king a "kingdom." One might say "the kingdom of the Persians," meaning the Persian region, or "the kingdom of the Romans." In the same way, Scripture there calls those who are ruled, the human race under his rule, a "kingdom." To see that this is true, hear how Scripture calls the nation that is ruled a "kingdom." When King Ahab was searching for the blessed prophet Elijah, his steward said: "As the Lord lives, there is no place and no nation to which my lord the king has not sent to look for you; he nearly set his kingdom on fire, and he did not find you." That is, he set on fire all who were ruled by him when he did not find you. Do you see that "kingdom" means not only the dignity but also the nations that are ruled? The Savior, then, hands over the kingdom. That kingdom is humanity, once ruled by sin and once ruled by death, which he rescues from captivity and wins back so that he may present it to God the Father. The divine Scriptures have shown beyond dispute that he was established king on Zion, that God gave him the throne of his father David, and that in this new kingship too he reigns over the house of Jacob forever. But he was king even before the incarnate dispensation and before the Passion. Before he received the throne of his father David according to the flesh, he had the throne that is before the ages. Isaiah will testify to this, saying: "And I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and the house was full of his glory." Further on he says: "Woe is me, wretch that I am! For I am a man with unclean lips, and I live among a people with unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord Sabaoth." Pay close attention to this testimony. When Isaiah saw God sitting on a throne as king, he says: "And I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord Sabaoth." Whom did he see? Of whom did he speak? Ask John the Evangelist, so that nothing is forced and everything is attested by the truth. What human reasoning has built, other reasoning overturns. But what the Holy Spirit has proclaimed through the mouths of prophets and apostles has no one to contradict it, and even when it has opponents, it proves its victory in the test. Whom, then, did Isaiah see? "And I have seen with my eyes," he says, "the King, the Lord Sabaoth." How did he see him? "Sitting on a throne, high and lifted up." And what did the Lord say to him? "And the Lord said to me: Go and say to this people, 'You will indeed hear, but never understand, and you will indeed see, but never perceive.' For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have become hard of hearing," and so on.

What, then, does John the Evangelist say? He is the great wing of theology, truly a son of thunder. On the dispensation he flashed like lightning, and on theology he thundered. He speaks about the Savior. Keep the passage in mind, so that the length of the discourse does not simply carry it past you, or rather, so that the number of words does not confuse your mind. "I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord," says Isaiah, "and he said to me: Go and say to this people, 'You hear indeed, but never understand.'" John then says: "Though Jesus had done so many signs, the Jews did not believe in him, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: Go and say to this people, 'You will indeed hear, but never understand,'" and so on. Someone might think that John took up the words only because they fit, as though the saying fit but the one Isaiah saw sitting on the throne was not the Son. To prevent this, the evangelist adds: "Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke about him." What glory? "I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high, and the house was full of his glory." Whom did he see? "And I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord Sabaoth." What king? The one to whom Nathanael cried out: "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel." This is what is wonderful. Those who listen diligently and eagerly will remember that we showed how Nathanael's cry agrees with the prophecy of Isaiah that says: "Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel." Elsewhere the same prophet says again: "Thus says the Lord God, the King of Israel, who redeemed him, the eternal God." You will also remember who the redeemer is, what the ransom is and how it was given: the body is the ransom, and the blood is the ransom. "Who redeemed him." Because of the dispensation, he seemed to have appeared only recently. So that people looking at the flesh would not be ignorant of the dignity of his Godhead, the prophet says: "Who redeemed him, the eternal God." The Father, then, is eternal, the Son is eternal and the Holy Spirit is eternal. Can the heretic not object again that this makes three eternal beings? "The Father is eternal," he said, "the Son is eternal, the Spirit is eternal." These are not three eternal natures but one eternal nature, made manifest in one Trinity. Hear what blessed Isaiah says: "The great God, the eternal, who fashioned the ends of the earth." Who fashioned them? If the heretic wants to escape the doctrine of the Son's divinity, he says, "This was said of the Father," and forgets his own words. For he says: "The Father made only the Son, and the Son made everything else." If the Son is the maker of all things, he also made the ends of the earth, for the one who fashioned the ends of the earth is the great, eternal God. But to expose their ignorance even more clearly, I will bring in blessed Paul as a witness that he calls the Son great God. He is great God because he is the Son of a great Father. As the begetter is, so is the begotten. If the begetter is small, the fruit of the root is small too. But if the Father is great, the Son is also great, for a great Father does not have a small son. "The eternal God, who fashioned the ends of the earth." Hear Paul saying: "The saving grace of God has appeared to all people. It trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly and godly in this present age, as we await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." (He says this in the Epistle to Titus.) "For the saving grace has appeared, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly and godly in this present age, as we await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." See: the great eternal God is the one who fashioned the ends of the earth, and the great eternal God is the one who came into the world. That is why David too says: "Great is our Lord, and great is his strength." For Christ is the power of God, and in Hebrew strength and power are the same word. God is great and Christ is great, as in "The great God, the eternal" and "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." So David sings of him in other words: "Great is our Lord, and great is his strength." "Great is our Lord." Is our Lord one thing and his strength another? No. The strength was the power, and Christ is the power of God. So our Lord is great, and Christ is great. See, then: you have a great eternal God, God the Son of the great eternal God. When this great and eternal God appeared to human beings, he took up flesh formed by the Holy Spirit. "For what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit." How, then, was the Spirit the maker? The Holy Spirit formed the temple of God the Word in that holy and great virgin. He came forth from the virgin with a body formed by the Holy Spirit through divine power, invisibly and ineffably. Where, then, is it shown that the Spirit is eternal? Hear blessed Paul saying: "For if the blood of bulls and goats and the sprinkled ashes of a heifer sanctify those who are defiled for the purification of the flesh." This refers to the sacrifices offered through Moses. That blood was once sprinkled, and it was a kind of initiation into a mystery that appeared one way but was understood mystically in another. Wishing to set spiritual things beside things perceived by the senses, and beside the true prayer [?], he says: "For if the blood of bulls and goats and the sprinkled ashes of a heifer sanctify those who are defiled for the purification of the flesh, how much more the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself to God." What does "through the eternal Spirit" mean? The Savior's flesh has the Holy Spirit as a kind of teacher. This is not because God the Word was too weak to guide the flesh. Rather, whatever God the Word did was ascribed to the Holy Spirit. Who drives out demons? Is it not God the Word? Yet God the Word says: "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God." He ascribes his own works to the Spirit, because there is one nature and the activity is undivided. Scripture testifies that that holy body was, as it were, led and guided by the activity of the Holy Spirit, when it says: "And it came to pass that when Jesus came up out of the water of the Jordan, he was led by the Spirit." What does "he was led" mean? It means that the flesh was guided: "He was led by the Spirit into the wilderness." That is why we too, in imitation of the Savior, are led. For Paul says: "If you are led by the Spirit of God, you are not under the law." That is why the Savior presents himself as the fountain of life and the Holy Spirit as living water. Do you see how he indicates that the essence is undivided? The Savior says: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly will flow rivers of water springing up to eternal life." At once John the Evangelist adds what the living water is: "He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed were going to receive."

Pay close attention. If, then, the Holy Spirit is living water, and it is this that believers receive, why did you say, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me,” and not, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to the Holy Spirit”? But even though I said “to me,” I spoke the truth. For there is one fountain of both: “For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light.” But since the Savior called the Holy Spirit living water, why does he say “living water”? So that you may learn that it is from the fountain of God. The Spirit is living water; God is the fountain of living water; so that when you learn what the fountain is, you may understand where the living water comes from. “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” And he said this of the water with reference to the Spirit, which those who believed were to receive. If the Spirit is living water, let us seek its fountain. What is the fountain? Let Jeremiah tell us: “Thus says the Lord: Heaven was astonished at this, and the earth shuddered, because my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water.” Do you see God as the fountain of water, and the Holy Spirit as living water? The Father is the fountain of living water; the Son is the river going forth from the earth; the Holy Spirit is the water of the river. “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water.” Let the prophet Isaiah also say the same about the Son: “And the Lord will come like a glorious river in a thirsty land.” Do you see the fountain? The river? The living water? Just as you cannot call the fountain a river so long as you are looking at the source, nor again can you call the river a fountain once it has gone forth, nor do you call the water that branches off from the river and irrigates the land a river, but irrigation water — and the names are divided, but the nature is undivided — so then (for I will take up the same points again and go through them), you do not call the fountain a river so long as you are looking at the source, nor, once the fountain has gone forth into a river, do you call it a fountain, but the outflow of that fountain; and again, when the river's water goes out for irrigation it is not called a river, but irrigating water; and the names are divided, but the nature is not divided. In the same way it is not possible to call the Father Son, nor the Son Father, lest we fall into the opinion of Sabellius. Yet the difference of names does not divide the nature. For the heretics want to build a difference of nature out of the difference of names. But when you see these images set side by side, do not be wholly a slave to the image. For nothing visible represents the invisible clearly. Rather, the images avoid what is absurd and take up what is glorious. For it does not follow that, because a river proceeds by outflow, the Father begot by a flowing. And I have said these things following Scripture. For no believer dares to speak on his own. If I had not heard the Father saying, “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water”; if I had not heard the Lord saying, “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” — and this he said about the Spirit, which those who believed were to receive — I would not have invented these things with human and mortal thought concerning the immortal nature. But let us come to a clearer demonstration. And let no one think this teaching superfluous. For above all, now that grace is drawing near, and since the living water is about to display its own working, he has placed an intelligible water within the waters. Indeed it must be spoken of in this way, both so that those who are coming forward may learn what kind of gift they are approaching, and so that those already counted worthy of the gift, as well as those who have not yet received it, may come to desire this gift. Necessarily, then, the holy and living water comes forth, proclaimed by word and worshiped by faith. Our Lord Jesus Christ calls the Holy Spirit living water, as he says to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” The prophets Zechariah and Ezekiel also speak about this water. Pay close attention. The Savior says to Nicodemus, the ruler of the Jews: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Nicodemus, being a Jew who had grown old in Jewish ignorance and was unable to imagine anything beyond bodily things, says to the Savior when he hears about rebirth: “How can these things be? Can a man who is old enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?” Hearing spiritual things, he took them in a bodily sense. The Savior says to him: “Everything born of the flesh is flesh.” I am not speaking about flesh, or about fleshly rebirth; “but what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” Then he rebukes him: “Are you the teacher of Israel, and do not know these things?” Do you see how serious a charge it is for one who holds the rank of teacher not to apply himself and search the Scriptures? “Are you the teacher of Israel, and do not know these things?” And if he was the teacher of Israel, how was he to know that you were proclaiming a strange mystery and a heavenly gift? For until now no one had proclaimed such a baptism of immortality. “Yes,” he says, “but the prophets made it known. Have you not read the prophets? Are you not a priest? Are you not a teacher? Have you not heard about water and spirit in the prophet? What strange thing have I said beyond the prophets in saying, ‘Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit’?” Ezekiel too spoke of these things: “And it shall be in the last days, says Adonai the Lord: I will take you to myself, and I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and I will put my Spirit within you.” Water and Spirit. “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit.” “I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and I will give you a new spirit.” Water and Spirit.

Again, the blessed Ezekiel, clearly depicting the regeneration to come, says: “And the hand of the Lord came upon me. And the Lord brought me out to the porch of the gate that faces east. And behold, water was coming out from the court toward the east.” Everywhere it is “toward the east,” since the fountain of salvation is from there. For just as his glory came from there, by the way that faces east, so too the water came from there. “And behold,” he says, “water was coming out from the court by the gate of the way that faces east. And the water came out, and behold, the appearance of a man. And he had a measure in his hand, and behold, as it were a man going out.” He saw water, and he also saw a man. “And the Lord brought me out to the gate that faces east, and behold, water was coming out from beneath the court.” Not even this is idle: “from beneath the court,” the open court. Nothing is covered; all is bare, pure, transparent, filled with light. “From beneath the court, from the right side toward the east; and behold, as it were a man going out.” It could not have been otherwise than “as it were a man going out.” A man came out together with the water, and it was a mystery. For the one signified the Savior's economy, the other the working of the Spirit. Water and a man: the incarnate economy and the working of the Spirit. “And a measure in his hand.” What measure? The measure of the gift. “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.” “And a measure in his hand.” Pay close attention, I beg you, so that you may know that the hope of immortality was announced from of old. “Behold, water was coming out, and as it were a man going out before me, and there was a measure in his hand.” What is the measure? Grace, and the measure of the gift. “And he measured a thousand in the water.” What does “a thousand” mean? He did not say cubits or reeds, but “a thousand.” Some things he says, others he conceals. “And he measured a thousand. And there passed through the water a water of remission.” “And he measured with the measure with which he measured, a thousand. And there passed through the water a water of remission.” What water of remission passed through the water? Since in baptism there is both perceptible water and intelligible water, the water of remission passed through the perceptible water; that is, the Spirit, who holds the remission of sins, passed through the perceptible water. “And there passed through the water a water of remission.” For where the Spirit is, there too is the forgiveness of sins, as the Savior says when he breathed on them: “Receive the Holy Spirit; if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them.” Then the prophet — or rather God through the prophet — wishing to show how the mystery of baptism begins from a few, but was going to multiply and cover the world: it begins first from Palestine through the twelve apostles; then it filled Palestine, filled Syria, went out to the east as well, reached the western regions too, and passed beyond to where the sun sets. Wishing to show this very thing, how the knowledge of the mystery was going to advance step by step, God says through the prophet: “He had a measure in his hand, and he measured a thousand; and there passed through the water a water of remission. And he measured another thousand, and the water rose up to the loins.” It advanced little by little. First water; then deep water rising up to the loins. “And he measured another thousand; and he could no longer pass through, because the water had increased. And the water was coming out, and it was a great river.” First water; then up to the loins; then a river. “And he measured a third time, a thousand” — a thousand, a thousand, a thousand. The number goes up to a thousand. For perfect is the name of the Father, and the name of the Son, and the name of the Holy Spirit. “And he measured a thousand; and there passed through the water a water of remission. And he measured another thousand, and the water rose up to the loins; and he measured a third time a thousand.” When the fullness of knowledge came, then the third was added. And the measure is one, but applied a third time; that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one Godhead, one power, one authority, proclaimed in three names. “And the water,” he says, “was increasing, like a flooding torrent.” What does “like a torrent” mean? The working of the Holy Spirit. He calls the succession of gifts, one upon another, a torrent. For a river that flows continually carries a quiet stream, but a torrent, swelling all at once, brings wave upon wave and sweeps everything away. So the God who loves mankind, wishing to show the gift of grace — that it is water of remission for those who believe, but flooding water for those who do not believe, sweeping away the error of demons, the tyranny of demons, the wickedness of the devil — says: “It came out like a flooding torrent.” What is the torrent? Hear God saying through Isaiah: “Behold, I turn toward them like a river, and like a flooding torrent.” A river for the faithful; a torrent for those who oppose him. And it passed like a torrent for those who oppose him, and those waters became like a flooding torrent. See how he explains the gift. What working does that water have? As the prophet says: “And waters came out, and on this side of the river and on that side of the river there were very great plants, and the waters were healing.” What does “and the waters were healing” mean? That it brings health. “See, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.” “And behold, trees on this side of the river and on that side of the river. And every soul to which the waters come will be healed. And there were many fish in the river.” What fish? The great multitude of people. “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men.” “And behold, many fish in the river, like the fish of the sea”; that is, the coming of Christ gathers as many as the whole inhabited world holds, like the fish in the great sea. Those whom the world held, the Church received. “And every tree” (again I repeat the passage) “on this side of the river and on that side of the river will spring up, and the waters will give life and will heal; and the fruit of the plants will not fail.” While Christ is being proclaimed, a lamp is brought in. For prophecies too are wont to light a lamp for Christ, as David says: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.” A visible lamp has arrived. Take note of the lamp, but attend to the matter at hand: “And there were many trees by the river, and the fruit of those trees will not fail, because of their newness.” For they were not old plants but new ones. He speaks of new plants, new fruits. “Put off the old man, and put on the new, which is being renewed.”

Do you see the grace foretold? Do you see how rightly the Lord rebuked Nicodemus: “Are you the teacher of Israel, and do not know these things?” But Zechariah bears witness to these things — not the father of John, of that John who once dwelt in the desert, adorned Palestine, and crowned our city. It befits John to cry out even after death, and to sing hymns from the tomb. For if he leapt in the womb and proclaimed the Master, he will leap from the tomb with his holy bones and say: “All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?” So the blessed Zechariah says: “And it shall be in the last of days that every place will be opened to the house of David.” By the house of David he means the kindred of David, since Joseph, the betrothed of Mary, was of the house of David: “betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house and lineage of David.” At the Savior's appearing every place was opened: east, west, south, north. “And it shall be in the last days that every place will be opened to the house of David, and living water will go out from Jerusalem.” What living water? “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” “And living water will go out from Jerusalem.” From where does it go out? “A word will go out from Jerusalem” — from where Christ came — “from Zion.” The living water comes from Jerusalem. And why from Jerusalem? Because from there the manifestation of the Spirit began: the apostles received the Holy Spirit in Jerusalem, and from there, through the apostles, it went forth to the ends of the earth. “So living water will go out from Jerusalem. Half of it to the first sea, and half of it to the last sea.” What did “to the first sea” and “to the last sea” mean? Does Scripture tell little fables? It proclaims truth, interprets mystery, reveals powers. “Living water will go out.” See the wonder. He does not say “a river,” but first “water.” For grace always begins from small things and multiplies into great ones. “Living water will go out from Jerusalem. Half of it to the first sea, and half of it to the last sea.” By the first sea he means the parts of the world that were inhabited first, in the east. For it was there that the race of Adam first flourished; then afterward it went out to the west and filled the world. So he calls the regions of the earth first inhabited the first sea, and the farthest parts of the west the last sea: the water both fills the east and honors the west. Consider, then, the mystery that the children of heretics laugh at, insulting the Holy Spirit and imposing the rank of a servant on a sovereign power. Let us flee wickedness, let us flee heretical blasphemy, let us flee also a life of base deeds. Doing good is proof of faith; love of others is proof of faith. Have mercy on the poor. Help, and receive; for you cannot reap what you do not sow. How can you say to God, “Forgive me”? How do you ask for what you do not give? How do you receive what you do not do? Remember, then, the words you spoke in your poverty. When you were poor and asked help from the poor, you used to say, “I wish I had something, and I would share it; I wanted to give; God knows my intention.” God often tests such a mind and exposes it by events themselves: he leads the man to wealth, and he no longer judges himself, but forgets his earlier words. For each person is truly judged by what he says. As long as we are not judges, we say: “If I were a judge, I would do this; if I were a judge, I would manage things this way; if I were a judge, I would decree this and that.” You have come to the judgment seat: show us your promise. When you were poor, you promised almsgiving, you promised just judgment. Now show the deeds as well. But in their lowly state people are like locusts. For in wintertime the locust sits on a hedge, unable even to feed; it is bound by the cold, and is lowly, easy to handle and easy to catch. But warmed a little by the sun it flies up, and the one that before could not rise from its place flies off into the air. So too a man is lowly in afflictions, devout, gentle, showing kindness. Then prosperity raised its head, and his disposition was laid bare. That is why Scripture says to the Jews, who were devout in misfortune but undevout in prosperity: “The locust leapt up like the grasshopper; your mixed multitude is like the locust. The sun rose, and it flew away and forgot its place.” He means the mixed people. “It leapt up like a locust, and like a locust settled on a hedge on a day of frost. The sun rose, and it flew away, and did not know its place”; that is, it forgot its lowliness. So we too are humble in poverty; we became rich, and we forgot. In the presence of death we philosophize, and when a corpse is carried out, everyone philosophizes about human affairs, saying, “All things pass away; we are nothing.” As long as he sees the [?], he philosophizes; once the frightening sight has gone, he immediately forgets his resolve. That is why Scripture says: “In all your words remember your last end, and you will never sin.” In all things remember your last end, and you will keep your mind unshaken. May it be granted to us, brothers, to remain faithful to God in all things, to whom belongs all glory, honor and might, to the ages of ages. Amen.
